transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Excuse me. Would you mind if I asked you some questions? We're doing a survey on transport.

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: Yes, that's OK.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: First of all, can I take your name?

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: Yes. It's Sadie Jones.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Thanks very much. And could I have your date of birth – just the year will do, actually. Is that all right?

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: Yes, that's fine. It's 1991.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: So next your postcode, please.

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: It's <q id="1">DW30 7YZ</q>.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Great. Thanks. Is that in Wells?

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: No it's actually in Harborne – Wells isn't far from there, though.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: I really like that area. My grandmother lived there when I was a kid.

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: Yes, it is nice.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Right, so now I want to ask you some questions about how you travelled here today. Did you use public transport?

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: Yes. I came by bus.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: OK. And that was today. It's the <q id="2">24th of April</q>, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: Isn't it the 25th? No, actually, you're right.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Ha ha. And what was the reason for your trip today? I can see you've got some shopping with you.

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: Yes. I did some shopping but the main reason I came here was to go to the <q id="3">dentist</q>.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: That's not much fun. Hope it was nothing serious.

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: No, it was just a check-up. It's fine.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Good. Do you normally travel by bus into the city centre?

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: Yes. I stopped driving in ages ago because <q id="4">parking</q> was so difficult to find and it costs so much.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: I see.

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: The bus is much more convenient too. It only takes about 30 minutes.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: That's good. So where did you start your journey?

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: At the bus stop on <q id="5">Claxby</q> Street.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Is that C-L-A–X-B-Y?

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: That's right.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: And how satisfied with the service are you? Do you have any complaints?

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: Well, as I said, it's very convenient and quick when it's on time, but this morning it was <q id="6">late</q>. Only about 10 minutes, but still.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: Yes, I understand that's annoying. And what about the timetable? Do you have any comments about that?

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: Mmm. I suppose I mainly use the bus during the day, but any time I've been in town in the <q id="7">evening</q> – for dinner or at the cinema – I've noticed you have to wait a long time for a bus – there aren't that many.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: OK, thanks. So now I'd like to ask you about your car use.

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: Well, I have got a car but I don't use it that often. Mainly just to go to the <q id="8">supermarket</q>. But that's about it really. My husband uses it at the weekends to go to the golf club.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: And what about a bicycle?

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: I don't actually have one at the moment.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: What about the city bikes you can rent? Do you ever use those?

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: No – I'm not keen on cycling there because of all the <q id="9">pollution</q>. But I would like to get a bike – it would be good to use it to get to work.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: So why haven't you got one now?

transcript.speaker: SADIE
transcript.text: Well, I live in a flat – on the second floor and it doesn't have any <q id="10">storage</q> – so we'd have to leave it in the hall outside the flat.

transcript.speaker: MAN
transcript.text: I see. OK. Well, I think that's all ...

Good evening, everyone. Let me start by welcoming you all to this talk and thanking you for taking the time to consider joining ACE voluntary organisation. ACE offers support to people and services in the local area and we're now looking for more volunteers to help us do this.

By the way, I hope you're all comfortable – <q id="11">we have brought in extra seats so that no one has to stand, but it does mean that the people at the back of the room may be a bit squashed.</q> We'll only be here for about half an hour so, hopefully, that's OK.

One of the first questions we're often asked is how old you need to be to volunteer. Well, <q id="12">you can be as young as 16 or you can be 60 or over;</q> it all depends on what type of voluntary work you want to do. <q id="12">Other considerations, such as reliability, are crucial</q> in voluntary work and age isn't related to these, in our experience.

Another question we get asked relates to training. Well, there's plenty of that and it's all face-to-face. What's more, <q id="13">training doesn't end when you start working for us – it takes place before, during and after periods of work.</q> Often, it's run by other experienced volunteers as managers tend to prefer to get on with other things.

Now, I would ask you to consider a couple of important issues before you decide to apply for voluntary work. We don't worry about why you want to be a volunteer – people have many different reasons that range from getting work experience to just doing something they've always wanted to do. But <q id="14">it is critical that you have enough hours in the day</q> for whatever role we agree is suitable for you – if being a volunteer becomes stressful then it's best not to do it at all. You may think that your income is important, but we don't ask about that. It's up to you to decide if you can work without earning money. <q id="15">What we value is dedication.</q> Some of our most loyal volunteers earn very little themselves but still give their full energy to the work they do with us.
OK, so let's take a look at some of the work areas that we need volunteers for and the sort of things that would help you in those.

You may wish simply to help us raise money. <q id="16">If you have the creativity to come up with an imaginative or novel way of fundraising, we'd be delighted,</q> as standing in the local streets or shops with a collection box can be rather boring!

One outdoor activity that we need volunteers for is <q id="17">litter collection and for this it's useful if you can walk for long periods, sometimes uphill.</q> Some of our regular collectors are quite elderly, but very active and keen to protect the environment!

If you enjoy working with children, we have three vacancies for what are called 'playmates'. These volunteers help children learn about staying healthy through a range of out-of-school activities. You don't need to have children yourself, but <q id="18">it's good if you know something about nutrition</q> and can give clear instructions.

If that doesn't appeal to you, maybe you would be interested in <q id="19">helping out at our story club for disabled children, especially if you have done some acting.</q> We put on three performances a year based on books they have read and we're always looking for support with the theatrical side of this.

The last area I'll mention today is first aid. Volunteers who join this group can end up teaching others in vulnerable groups who may be at risk of injury. Initially, though, your priority will be <q id="20">to take in a lot of information and not forget any important steps or details.</q>
Right, so does anyone have any questions …

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: Hi Chantal. What did you think of the talk, then?

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: Hi Hugo. I thought it was good once I'd moved seats.

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: Oh – were the people beside you chatting or something?

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: It wasn't that. I went early so that I'd get a seat and not have to stand, but then <q id="21">this guy sat right in front of me and he was so tall!</q>

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: <q id="21">It's hard to see through people's heads, isn't it?</q>

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: Impossible! Anyway, to answer your question, I thought it was really interesting, especially what the speaker said about the job market.

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: Me too. I mean we know we're going into a really competitive field so it's obvious that we may struggle to get work.

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: That's right – and we know we can't all have that 'dream job'.

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: Yeah, but <q id="22">it looks like there's a whole range of … areas of work that we hadn't even thought of</q> – like fashion journalism, for instance.

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: Yeah – I wasn't expecting so many career options.

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: Mmm. Overall, she had quite a strong message, didn't she?

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: She did. She kept saying things like 'I know you all think this, but …' and then she'd tell us how it really is.

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: Perhaps she thinks students are a bit narrow-minded about the industry.

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: <q id="23">It was a bit harsh, though! We know it's a tough industry.</q>

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: <q id="23">Yeah – and we're only first years, after all. We've got a lot to learn.</q>

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: Exactly. Do you think our secondary-school education should have been more career-focused?

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: Well, we had numerous talks on careers, which was good, but <q id="24">none of them were very inspiring. They could have asked more people like today's speaker to talk to us.</q>

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: I agree. We were told about lots of different careers – just when we needed to be, but not by the experts who really know stuff.

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: So did today's talk influence your thoughts on what career you'd like to take up in the future?

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: <q id="25">Well, I promised myself that I'd go through this course and keep an open mind till the end.</q>

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: <q id="25">But I think it's better to pick an area of the industry now and then aim to get better and better at it.</q>

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: <q id="26">Well, I think we'll just have to differ on that issue!</q>

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: One thing's for certain, though. From what she said, we'll be unpaid assistants in the industry for quite a long time.

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: Mmm.

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: <q id="26">I'm prepared for that, aren't you?</q>

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: Actually, I'm not going to accept that view.

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: Really? But she knows it's the case – and everyone else says the same.

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: That doesn't mean it has to be true for me.

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: OK. Well – I hope you're right!

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: I thought the speaker's account of her first job was fascinating.

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: Yeah – she admitted she was lucky to get work being a personal dresser for a musician. She didn't even apply for the job and there she was getting paid to choose all his clothes.

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: It must have felt amazing – though she said all she was looking for back then was experience, not financial reward.

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: Mmm. And then he was so mean, <q id="27">telling her she was more interested in her own appearance than his!</q>

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: But – <q id="28">she did realise he was right about that,</q> which really made me think. I'm always considering my own clothes but now I can see you should be focusing on your client!

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: She obviously regretted losing the job.

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: Well, as she said, <q id="28">she should have hidden her negative feelings about him, but she didn't.</q>

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: It was really brave the way she picked herself up and took that job in retail. Fancy working in a shop after that!

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: Yeah – well, she recommended we all do it at some point. I guess as a designer you'd get to find out some useful information, like how big or small the average shopper is.

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: I think that's an issue for manufacturers, not designers. However, <q id="29">it would be useful to know if there's a gap in the market – you know, an item that no one's stocking but that consumers are looking for.</q>

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: Yeah, people don't give up searching. They also take things back to the store if they aren't right.

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: Yeah. Imagine you worked in an expensive shop and <q id="30">you found out the garments sold there were being returned because they … fell apart in the wash!</q>

transcript.speaker: CHANTAL
transcript.text: Yeah, it would be good to know that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: HUGO
transcript.text: Yeah.

For my presentation today I want to tell you about how groups of elephants have been moved and settled in new reserves. This is known as translocation and has been carried out in Malawi in Africa in recent years. The reason this is being done is because of overpopulation of elephants in some areas.

Overpopulation is a good problem to have and not one we tend to hear about very often. In Malawi's Majete National Park the elephant population had been wiped out by poachers, who killed the elephants for their ivory. But in 2003, the park was restocked and effective law enforcement was introduced. Since then, not a single elephant has been poached. In this safe environment, the elephant population boomed. Breeding went so well that there were more elephants than the park could support.

This led to a number of problems. Firstly, there was more competition for food, which meant that some elephants were suffering from hunger. As there was a limit to the amount of food in the national park, some elephants began looking further afield. <q id="31">Elephants were routinely knocking down fences around the park</q>, which then had to be repaired at a significant cost.

To solve this problem, the decision was made to move dozens of elephants from Majete National Park to Nkhotakota Wildlife Park, where there were no elephants. But, obviously, attempting to move significant numbers of elephants to a new home 300 kilometres away is quite a challenge.
So how did this translocation process work in practice?

Elephants were moved in <q id="32">groups of between eight and twenty, all belonging to one family.</q> Because relationships are very important to elephants, they all had to be moved at the same time. <q id="33">A team of vets and park rangers flew over the park in helicopters and targeted a group, which were rounded up and directed to a designated open plain.</q>

The vets then used darts to immobilise the elephants – this was a tricky manoeuvre, as they not only had to select the right dose of tranquiliser for different-sized elephants but they had to dart the elephants as they were running around. <q id="34">This also had to be done as quickly as possible so as to minimise the stress caused.</q> As soon as the elephants began to flop onto the ground, the team moved in to take care of them.

<q id="35">To avoid the risk of suffocation, the team had to make sure none of the elephants were lying on their chests because their lungs could be crushed in this position. So all the elephants had to be placed on their sides.</q> One person stayed with each elephant while they waited for the vets to do checks. <q id="36">It was very important to keep an eye on their breathing – if there were fewer than six breaths per minute, the elephant would need urgent medical attention.</q> Collars were fitted to the matriarch in each group so their movements could be tracked in their new home. <q id="37">Measurements were taken of each elephant's tusks – elephants with large tusks would be at greater risk from poachers – and also of their feet.</q> The elephants were then taken to a recovery area before being loaded onto trucks and transported to their new home.

The elephants translocated to Nkhotakota settled in very well and the project has generally been accepted to have been a huge success – and not just for the elephants. <q id="38">Employment prospects have improved enormously, contributing to rising living standards for the whole community.</q> Poaching is no longer an issue, as former poachers are able to find more reliable sources of income. In fact, <q id="39">many of them volunteered to give up their weapons, as they were no longer of any use to them.</q>

More than two dozen elephants have been born at Nkhotakota since relocation. With an area of more than 1,800 square kilometres, there's plenty of space for the elephant population to continue to grow. Their presence is also helping to rebalance Nkhotakota's damaged ecosystem and providing a sustainable conservation model, which could be replicated in other parks. <q id="40">All this has been a big draw for tourism, which contributes five times more than the illegal wildlife trade to GDP, and this is mainly because of the elephants.</q> There's also been a dramatic rise in interest …
